MR. MACKASEY-REPORTED SPEECH BY MEMBER FOR QU'APPELLE
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege stemming from a news report which appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of March 2 on page 6. The article in question covers a political rally in that city at which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was the main speaker. I should like to quote part of that article to which I take grave exception:
"Not all problems in Canada are confined to rural people," he reminded some 75 delegates to a prairie regional seminar of the young Progressive Conservatives and the Progressive Conservative student federation.
"Who speaks up for the people in the eastern part of Montreal-this garbage can type of member we've got from there?"
As a member representing a riding on the island of Montreal I resent very sincerely the inference which can be drawn from the remarks of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I consider them a reflection not only on myself and on the Montreal members, but in the final analysis, a reflection on all members in this house and an indication of the type of sickness which is permeating the Canadian political scene. I would remind the hon. member that his remarks include the hon. member for St. Mary, who to the best of my knowledge has always fulfilled his role with dignity and honesty; and I would urge him, taking into consideration his enthusiasm at political rallies, to kindly restrict his remarks, or at least to have the courtesy to identify the member or members to whom he chooses to refer.

subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-REPORTED SPEECH BY MEMBER FOR QU'APPELLE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Indeed, I recall reading an editorial in one of the newspapers last Friday calling on the federal Liberal party to clean up this situation.

subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-REPORTED SPEECH BY MEMBER FOR QU'APPELLE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-REPORTED SPEECH BY MEMBER FOR QU'APPELLE
speechtext: If my remarks have caused harm to the hon. member for Verdun or, for that matter, to any individual member from the island of Montreal, I sincerely apologize. But I want to make it very clear that as all of us in this house know, the situation in Montreal does bring blame to us all and I would join, I hope, with the hon. member in asking that all those who are associating anywhere with the type of thing we are now experiencing in Canada should help clear it up. I would think the party to which the hon. member belongs would do better for the public if it did some clearing up in its house at the present time rather than raising questions of privilege such as the hon. member has just raised.

MR. PERRON-REPLY BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING STATUS OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises from the fact that members of parliament have a right to know the truth about statements made in the house by the Prime Minister.
As reported on page 11972 of Hansard of March 4 the following question was asked by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey):
Mr. Speaker, the second part of my question was simply this. Does the government of the day recognize the special constitutional status of the province of Quebec?
The Prime Minister gave an answer which I personally heard, which other hon. members also heard and which would appear to have been heard by parliamentary correspondents according to the news report published by the Canadian Press. This news report was reproduced in practically every daily newspaper in the province of Quebec on Friday March 5 under the title:
Quebec has always enjoyed special status, according to Mr. Pearson.
I should also like to quote the following statement which appeared as subtitle for the article published in L'Action on March 5,1965:
Prime Minister Pearson stated yesterday that Quebec has always enjoyed a special status within the Canadian constitution.

Question of Privilege
Here is the answer given by the right hon. Prime Minister as reported in Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec has its present constitutional status inside our federal system, and the government recognizes that.
That gives a very different meaning to the reply. As hon. members and representatives of the press can see, the reply does not have the same meaning. Consequently, in order to set the record straight and to give words their proper meaning, not the one that a person might wish them to have, I would ask the Prime Minister to clarify the reply which is printed in Hansard or to state whether hon. members and parliamentary correspondents have misunderstood him when he said that Quebec has always enjoyed a special status and that constitutional amendments would always be possible if they became desirable.
Therefore, I ask this straight question: Does the government recognize a special status for the province of Quebec under the constitution?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR ST. DENIS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-TABLING OF REPORTS OF CONTROL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the text of the special message of February 13 from the international commission for supervision and control in Viet Nam reporting on the recent air strikes against North Viet Nam and on the directly related problem of North Viet Nam's long standing and continuing aggressive interference in South Viet Nam which gave rise to the air strikes in question. This report was released this morning in London by one of the co-chairmen of the Geneva accord powers, the secretary of state for foreign affairs in the United Kingdom.
This message comprises a majority report by India and Poland which deals only with
Viet Nam Control Commission the air strikes in early February, a minority statement by Canada which outlines some essential background to these air strikes, and finally separate Indian and Polish statements commenting on the position taken by Canada.
While not denying the facts on which the majority report is based, the Canadian government believes it presents an over-simplified and misleading impression of the root causes of the dangerous instability in Viet Nam. To correct such an impression the Canadian delegation has appended a statement to the majority report in the hope that the special message as a whole might reflect more accurately the full scope of the problem in Viet Nam. As both the Prime Minister and I have made clear on several occasions, the factor which underlies the grave situation in that country is the determined and long standing attempt of the Hanoi regime to bring South Viet Nam under its control through the pursuit of aggressive policies.
This factor has, of course, been evident to the international commission in Viet Nam for some time. The commission's special report of June 2, 1962 presented a balanced account of the situation by drawing attention to northern violations of the Geneva agreement and also the military assistance the United States was giving South Viet Nam at the latter's request to combat northern interference. I should like to table the main text, in English and in French, of the 1962 special report, since parliament was not in session at the time of its release.
That report's conclusion that North Viet Nam had violated the Geneva agreement by aggressive policies toward South Viet Nam was based on the work of the commission's legal committee, which had examined a vast amount of material relating to allegations of armed and unarmed intervention in South Viet Nam over a number of years. In the special report the commission undertook to take action on the basis of a fuller report to be prepared by its legal committee. Faced since then with the unwillingness of our commission colleagues to act on these promises, we have decided that it was necessary to go ahead on our own to fulfil these obligations.
The most significant conclusions of this legal study have therefore been quoted in paragraph 3 of the Canadian statement of February 13. These indicate quite clearly that the so-called South Viet Nam liberation front, of which the Viet Cong are in effect the armed forces, is a creature of the ruling party of North Viet Nam, that it is their

Viet Nam Control Commission common aim to bring about the violent overthrow of the South Vietnamese administration, and that the ruling party in North Viet Nam has assisted its agents in South Viet Nam in attempting to attain this objective. I think I hardly need underline what these conclusions mean for the theory one often hears developed, that the war in South Viet Nam is essentially an internal revolt.
Both the Indian and Polish representatives on the commission have questioned the status of the extracts of the legal committee's report quoted in the Canadian statement. I cannot agree that a document which has been carefully prepared by a properly constituted committee of the commission, acting on a majority basis, in pursuance of commission instructions and on the basis of material referred to it by the commission, has no status.
The Polish representative has also questioned our right to quote from and append some recent South Vietnamese allegations, which were directed in the normal manner to the commission for consideration. The allegations concerned do not, of course, pretend to be commission conclusions. According to these complaints, however, large quantities of arms, munitions and supplies of communist origin, and large numbers of military personnel have been steadily infiltrated into South Viet Nam from the north by land and sea, and secret bases and related installations have been established by the Viet Cong with the support of North Viet Nam. To omit reference to them in current commission reports would imply that the commission had not been apprised of them or that it was totally ignoring the major complaints of one of the two parties to the Geneva agreement. The commission's silence since 1962 on the problem of subversion does not mean there has been any change for the better. On the contrary, judging by the evidence presented to the commission-and there is a large quantity of material of more recent origin now being reviewed by the commission's legal experts-it seems obvious that the hostile activities of the Hanoi regime have been steadily increasing.
Our independent observer position in Viet Nam has brought us face to face with an insidious form of aggression with which the free world has yet to devise adequate means of dealing. We have seen a new political entity emerge from colonial status only to be forced into a cruel struggle for survival against hostile pressures beyond its control.


In whatever form aggression manifests itself, it must be recognized as such and it must be stopped, not least because we cannot afford to let the practitioners of this technique come to the conclusion that it pays dividends.
This is surely the basic issue at stake in Viet Nam today, and it is of vital interest to all members of the international community. This is what we, by virtue of our membership on the international commission, have established as the lesson of the past ten years. I think it is important for all of us to have this fact clear in our minds before we go on to the next and most vital task, which is to attempt to restore peace to that troubled area. And here I must stress that I do not believe that the answer which all concerned could accept lies either in escalation and allout war or, on the other hand, surrender to communist pressures.
We are all deeply concerned with the implications for world peace, no less than for the future of the Vietnamese people of the continuation of the present situation. It contains the seeds of escalation and the dangers -all too evident to us today-of an open conflict of stark and terrifying proportions. As I have indicated on many occasions, we seek a peaceful and equitable solution, and our efforts are certainly being directed to that end. This is our immediate objective, to avoid the inevitable consequences of escalation. Clearly and firmly but without panic or alarm we must make our concern known to all-I repeat all-the direct participants in this conflict, always remembering that conditions on the ground, the actual deployment of power, will have an important influence on the willingness of the parties concerned to modify their policies. Only if all concerned are prepared to face up to their responsibilities and obligations and only if all concerned are prepared to exercise the restraint for which we and other nations have appealed can we take the next step toward the peaceful settlement which is our ultimate objective.
Finally, a satisfactory solution would be one which adequately protects and guarantees the independence of people who wish to remain independent. The 1954 Geneva agreements were designed to end war but failed to create a durable settlement and lasting peace. Canada has become acutely aware of the painful shortcomings of the 1954 settlement through more than ten years of experience in Indochina, where we have

been forced to observe the slow erosion of the terms of a cease fire agreement.
Perhaps a new and better arrangement could be achieved by some form of guaranteed neutrality, or through a stronger supervisory and policing mechanism capable of preventing aggressive interference from outside. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, this is surely an international responsibility. To discharge it, the lessons of the past indicate that there will be required an international presence involving more authority and more freedom of action than have obtained in the past, and this must be balanced by a mutual acceptance of this machinery and a readiness to co-operate in using it. It is clear that to be charged with supervision, yet to be powerless to check the slow erosion of a settlement, is not enough.
It is not easy in present circumstances to define the framework within which new and stronger mechanisms could be brought into being. While the United Nations might be considered as providing an obvious basis on which a new approach might be built up, attitudes thus far have tended to lessen the acceptability of this framework and the chances of its being successfully used. It cannot, however, be entirely excluded as one possibility. Another might well be the sort of grouping of more directly involved nations which were represented at Geneva in 1954 and 1962. At this juncture I do not believe it is as important to determine the eventual framework within which a settlement might be arranged as it is to try to ascertain whether there is any willingness and real basis for new negotiations.
The Canadian government for one intends to continue using all means at its disposal to see if the prerequisites for negotiation exist, and where possible to help create those conditions. If negotiations can be arranged- let me repeat it is our hope that conditions conducive to such negotiations will be encouraged by all possible means-our extended experience in the field in Indochina will help us to be of assistance in making concrete and practical proposals as to how the Geneva or any alternative machinery could be developed to achieve a lasting and peaceful settlement.
I may say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I have noted the comments made in the majority report by the representatives from India and Poland.
Viet Nam Control Commission

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR ST. DENIS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-TABLING OF REPORTS OF CONTROL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at once that I feel the statement made by the minister does not provide that framework of knowledge or information which the people are asking for at this time. I say this in a spirit of desire to bring about, if possible, a bipartisan policy in connection with this matter. The statement made by the minister was too general, too ephemeral and lacked the kind of information to which the Canadian people are entitled.
I know the difficulty of the government. We found ourselves in 1962, at the time of the Cuban trouble, having to face up to our responsibilities as Canadians. Some said we should have said, in words used in 1922 in regard to the Charnak incident, "Ready, aye ready." We took the stand in 1962 that we should ask the United States, while recognizing its responsibilities to preserve this hemisphere from communism, to act with that restraint with which power that is overwhelming, can always act. To place Canada in the position-that our critics urged-that we would say, "Whatever or wherever you lead we follow," was no policy for Canada.
I say today, after listening to the statement of the hon. gentleman, that I am more convinced than ever that we should have a day set aside for debate on this subject. There are those who criticize the United States and contend that the United States in its policy will bring escalation into general war. There are others who are pressing the United States to go further than it has gone. As the world leader for freedom, the United States is in a dreadful dilemma. On the one hand, if that country proceeds in a way that will bring communist China in to a greater extent than now, and will bring about a greater interest on the part of the U.S.S.R. in the problems of Viet Nam than now, then the frightful prospect of potential war faces not only the United States but all mankind.
The United States has in recent months been conducting a series of raids against concentrations, I think some 4,800 of them. It has stepped up its assistance to South Viet Nam to meet what the minister admits is a never ending infiltration from North Viet Nam and even beyond, I would say, from the volunteer communist Chinese reinforcements. Any action in this regard will accelerate the possibility of international war. On the other hand, anyone who has been in southeast Asia recognizes the fact that evacuation by the United States at this time, in the face of an

Viet Nam Control Commission unusual infiltration and an intensification of cold war tactics by the communists, will mean that not only southeast Asia but the whole of that area will fall ultimately to these tactics.
I should have liked to hear the minister deal with the position of the United States. After all, it has assumed the responsibility, by force of circumstances, of taking the position that Great Britain took for so long in all parts of the world. The United States today is in a position analogous to that of a fly in a spider's web. It is a fearful position. The United States, if one could borrow the classical allusion, finds itself in a position, whichever stand it takes, of the danger of shipwreck on Scylla or Charybdis. I would like to hear from the minister what course it should take, because the risks become of increasing measure day by day.
What course will Canada take? What is the attitude of Canada? The minister has tabled the minority report which, after all, does not go very far. It answers some of the criticisms that are inherent in the views expressed by the Indian and Polish representatives, but it does not meet the problem that faces the United States, as I see it the most difficult one that any nation has faced in the western world over a period of nine years.
What is the United States to do? It is easy to criticize. The communists are doing that; some of their friends in other parts of the world are doing that. Last week at the meeting of the 19 communist party leaders in Moscow they agreed on one thing, the denunciation of what the United States is doing, and interpreting what is being done as a deliberate policy of expanding the war. We in Canada, regardless of our fears, cannot accept that theory. We cannot accept the threat inherent in Mr. Gromyko's words, when he said:
If the American policymakers think they will frighten anyone by their bombings of North Viet Nam, they are deeply mistaken.
What should be done? I think the house should be taken into the confidence of the government, for if what is taking place expands into the wider field of armed conflict, Canada will have a greater interest in this matter than mere membership on a commission or the issuing of a minority report.
The minority report, as I summarize it, is simply to the effect that the situation in Viet Nam is dangerously unstable, that recent
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

events and particularly the bombing raids have provided, and I quote:
-a dramatic demonstration of this continuing condition.
It goes on to say, however, that the responsibility for what is taking place is that of North Viet Nam and its unnamed allies. It is the result of-
-the deliberate and persistent pursuit of aggressive but largely covert policies by North Viet Nam directed against South Viet Nam.
What is Canada going to do? There were great generalities in the speech of the Prime Minister in New York. There was the expression on the part of the government of its desire for peace. There was no answer to the question as to whether there is any basis for settlement that will help those peoples who rely on assistance from outside to preserve them from communism.
There is nothing to indicate whether there is still any belief that the partitions of the 1954 agreement are possible to maintain. Everybody says, why not negotiate? No one is able to give any answer as to the basis for negotiation. If I understood his speech aright, the Prime Minister suggested that we should have another peace keeping force sent, such as we had in Suez, in Korea and in Cyprus. How large would that force have to be? The North Viet Nam army is very large. The South Viet Nam army has some 300,000 men, and 100,000 are being added besides the assistance that comes from the United States. There has been an escalation in the number of Americans engaged there. I believe the United States started out by thinking 300 would be enough, but now the number is up in the thousands.
What kind of a force could be set up? How large would it have to be to discharge its responsibilities in an area where there are so many armed forces? Directly across the boundary between North Viet Nam and communist China there are, I am told, eight divisions of communist troops which act as training organizations for the North Vietnamese.
I expressed the thought the other day that statements such as were made by the Prime Minister in New York should have been made here in parliament, and I repeat that they should not be made elsewhere. When one analyses what took place on reading that speech, the question arises whether it was seriously taken into consideration in the United States. Certainly there is no reference

to it in the foreign affairs section or the editorial portion of the New York Sunday Times. What is this plan? Is it simply a warmed over peace force such as we had in Suez?
We certainly want more than a framework of suggestions. How many Canadian troops did the Prime Minister assure Secretary General Thant would be available? Any? Where are these forces coming from? Are they going to be recruited now or are they going to be taken from the detachments in Cyprus and elsewhere? Did the Prime Minister, when speaking with Mr. U Thant, give any assurance that in addition to men, financial assistance was going to be provided to this peace force?
These are the questions that occur to one, and the answers can only be ascertained through the medium of debate. Did the Prime Minister receive any response to his proposal? On that score I read from a United Nations dispatch, as reproduced in the Toronto Telegram, that the Prime Minister's "peace force idea was as obsolete as a model T Ford" in the conditions that exist in Viet Nam and southeast Asia.
What reaction did Canada get from the secretary general? What discussions have been initiated and with what powers for the provision of the necessary men? Has there been any indication from either Hanoi or Peking which would give any ground for the hope that the proposal in question would even receive consideration? I hope these questions will be answered, for all we have secured to date is an addition built on the framework of the speech which the Prime Minister made in New York on Friday; and I think that speech certainly qualified as setting forth a framework. But nothing has been placed before the house to indicate what is Canada's stand.
It is a terrible problem. It is one which exercises the hearts of free men everywhere. But, sir, and I say this with great respect to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, what we have received today is simply a mass of generalization without any supporting evidence to indicate that what was placed before that meeting in New York and, quite indirectly, said by the minister this afternoon, represents a practical solution to the problems facing us. Certainly the Canadian people are entitled to more than this.
I do not belong to the school which believes we should become a caboose on the United States train. I made that clear, and
Viet Nam Control Commission was criticized for doing so, when I was prime minister. On the other hand what is Canada's stand, accepting the basis of what has been said today, but the expression of a hope? I would add one more hope, namely that we shall be given an opportunity of debating the subject, of finding out what is the situation and what contribution Canada can make. France has its view. Forty and more Labour members in the United Kingdom have joined in criticism of their leader, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, for his stand supporting the United States. The communist countries are criticizing, and we expect them to.
We in the western world need greater knowledge than we have in respect to all the circumstances and plans for meeting the most fearsome prospect which the western world has faced for years. On the one hand, are millions of people-and I am not speaking of the population of South Viet Nam but of those in all southeast Asia who have stood against communism-to be left, so to speak, in the air? How long would they survive if the United States permitted itself the luxury of going back on its undertaking? On the other hand, how long will freedom survive if we in our country and other countries in the western world do not arrive at some basis of negotiation which will bring about at least an armistice in a very difficult situation?

speechtext:
Yes, I think that is correct. An hon. member behind me says he was followed by a close second in the person of the leader of the official opposition. But I will give the minister credit for being a most genial and well intentioned person.
We welcome the opportunity to study these reports carefully. However, judging by the information we have been able to secure from the press to date we are surprised to

Viet Nam Control Commission learn that the minority report of the Canadian government team apparently supports the action of the United States government in Viet Nam, that is to say the intention to negotiate when it can do so from a position of strength. What does that mean? Members of this group are anxious to know when the Canadian government intends to speak up without equivocation on this issue and support those in the United States and in other western countries who oppose this hopeless and dangerous war in South Viet Nam. When shall we support the efforts of men like Senator Church, Senator McGee and Senator Wayne Morse, as well as responsible members of the press both in the United States and in other western countries?
I may say that a good many Canadians are very concerned about this situation, because they realize that this government is today supporting United States foreign policy with respect to Viet Nam and they know this has possibly become a question, now, of peace or war. I do not intend to speak at great length, but I do wish to draw the attention of the house to a statement made in the Wall Street Journal of February 8 by Mr. Philip Geyelin-yes, the Wall Street Journal
in support of peace on this occasion. It reads as follows:
Clamor for a negotiated peace was growing in congress, among key allies and even within administration councils. In this atmosphere, the latest, most brazen guerrilla blow at a U.S. installation in South Viet Nam struck many U.S. policymakers, for many different reasons, as just the sort of provocation they have been looking for.
I mentioned the stand taken by some of the senators in the United States. Their voices are growing louder every day and support for them is increasing every day. Senator Church said on one occasion:
I submit, with all deference to the state department, that there has not yet been a consistent, clear-cut definition of the American purpose.
The senator goes on to criticize United States policy in this area. So does Senator McGee, and Senator Wayne Morse has done so on a number of occasions, as have others. Then we see in the Gazette of February 19, 1965 an interesting article by Mr. Walter Lippmann entitled "Viet Nam Debate" in which he says:
Apart from the question of the morality and the gigantic risks of escalating the war, there is no sufficient reason to think that the northern communists can be bombed into submission. We must not forget that North Viet Nam has a large army-larger, it is said, than any other army on the east Asian mainland except China's. This North Vietnamese army can walk and nobody has yet

found a way of bombing that can prevent foot soldiers from walking.
Then in another place he goes on to say:
For this country to involve itself in such a war in Asia would be an act of supreme folly. While the warhawks would rejoice when it began, the people would weep before it ended. There is no tolerable alternative except a negotiated truce, and the real problem is not whether we should negotiate but whether we can.
Then in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch of March 3 I find the following; the Post-Dispatch is critical of the intervention of the United States government in South Viet Nam:
The U.S. government has said that massive supplies of weapons are sent from North Viet Nam into South Viet Nam to help the Viet Cong rebels. The fact is that more than 75 per cent of the rebels' weapons are made in the U.S. and captured from the U.S.-backed troops of the Saigon government. Only a handful of Chinese weapons have been found in South Viet Nam.
The U.S. says that the Viet Cong (who actually call themselves the national liberation front), are communists. The fact is that most of the Viet Cong are not communists. They have followed communist leadership because the communists led the fight against the Japanese invaders in world war II; later, they led the fight against the French attempt at recolonization after world war II.
The Viet Cong are fighting now against the official government in Saigon because it is a dictatorship opposed by most of the people, and because it has not provided honest government or needed reforms.
The Viet Cong are fighting against the U.S. because we back the Saigon government, and because they want us out of Viet Nam.

I have read the interesting report of the Prime Minister's speech in the United States with respect to his discussions with U Thant. I must say, personally again, that I think the plan proposed by him was most ambiguous and very fuzzy indeed.
We believe it is reasonable that Canadian citizens should raise their voices against certain policies and actions of the government of the United States which we consider unrealistic and dangerous to the peace of Canada and the whole world. Once again we urge the Canadian government to speak out with a clear and firm voice for an immediate cease Are in the war conducted by the United States in Viet Nam. We urge the Canadian government to seek the reconvening of the 1954 Geneva conference in order to promote a negotiated settlement satisfactory to the people of Viet Nam and satisfactory to the
Viet Nam Control Commission people of the world. We believe the time is very appropriate for action in that direction. What we need is leadership in this respect, and a positive policy.
The danger that now faces mankind is that the war in Viet Nam may erupt into a world thermalnuclear war, threatening the very existence of the human race. We plead with the government to do everything possible within its power now to prevent such a calamity. After we have had the opportunity to read the two documents tabled by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the government will provide time for this house to discuss this very urgent question. This question is of prime importance and serious concern to the people of Canada and the rest of the world.

maintopic: MR. GREGOIRE-REPORTED STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR ST. DENIS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-TABLING OF REPORTS OF CONTROL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that words of commendation and congratulation are due to the Canadian representatives on the international control commission for having had the courage to bring out the facts as they saw them, in their responsibilities as one of three members of this control commission, when the other members in their majority report obviously did not bring out all that should have been said about the situation in Viet Nam. In view of the fact that there has not been agreement in this international control commission for the last two years-and in fact, as the minister stated, there has been no report from them since June, 1962-I believe it was the only honourable thing the Canadian members of the control commission could do, even if it meant taking a stand quite at variance, in some areas, with that of the other members of the commission.
The fact that they would be willing to stand alone in order to reveal certain facts is certainly something for which we should be grateful to them. Obviously the other members of the control commission are not free agents to express the situation as they see it. I believe we should take note of that, because otherwise what has been going on in the traffic of arms and personnel from China itself, through North Viet Nam into South Viet Nam, would have been talked about officially long before this.
This is not the time for lengthy debate, and I think we should keep our remarks strictly to the subject matter that has been raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs at this time. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I do believe the importance of this question is such that we must clarify it and clear away

Viet Nam Control Commission any cobwebs that may surround our thinking, which might lead us to believe that something else is taking place there other than what is actually taking place.
I would say that the entire military picture in Viet Nam today, which actually amounts to a full scale war, is such only because North Viet Nam has refused to accept the agreements that were laid down in 1954 by the Geneva agreement. If North Viet Nam was not disregarding those agreements and had not, ever since 1954, been seeking to take over South Viet Nam as a communist state, we never would have had the problem that is there today. All that is needed to have it settled is for North Viet Nam to withdraw its pressure and respect the boundary between North and South Viet Nam, and the American troops could go home; and I think they would, because I do not believe they have any interest there except to try to prevent the complete take-over of the world by communism. To say anything else is, I think, to disregard the facts of the case. Again, Mr. Speaker, if North Viet Nam would respect the 1954 agreements which the international control commission was supposed to supervise, we would not have the dangerous situation that we have now.
Second, I believe we cannot allow those who would take over the world in the name of communism to think they can obtain their objectives by the threat of force, by subversion, by infiltration, by ruthless guerrilla war, believing that those in the western world who oppose them will back down and appease. To do so would be a repetition of the events of 1938. In fact I think we are in a much more dangerous position in the world today than many of us realize, a situation which has many parallels with the situation which was developing in 1938 and the first nine months of 1939. Negotiation with and appeasement of the communists will lead us exactly where we went at that time. The hon. member for Kootenay West talked about being in support of peace. We are all in support of peace, but we will never get peace by appeasement. Any negotiation with the communists, particularly the Chinese communists, amounts to nothing less than appeasement.
Therefore we must be very careful in our condemnation of the United States. To say that we are following along like a little caboose and saying "Yes, yes" to their policies is to deny the facts of a very serious situation. While we cannot agree with all the policies of the United States, and think they 
are prone to error when they should not be, nevertheless we can be thankful that they are at least willing to stand up, when some other parts of the world are not willing to-do so, against the aggression of communism.
It is not a matter of numbers which properly settles any question or problem of morality. It has been said that the majority of arms used in South Viet Nam today are American arms. Yet in the minority report which was tabled today we read that over the past three or four years there has been a constant flow of arms and ammunition passing from China and North Viet Nam into South Viet Nam. To say that the Viet Cong are struggling for their own free government and autonomy is rather paradoxical when the fact has been brought out that about 90 per cent of the Viet Cong are not even South Vietnamese but come from North Viet Nam, and many of them come from China as well. Why has the international control commission, including our Canadian member, been kicked out of North Viet Nam? Because it stands in the way and is a threat to the military traffic and action which has been emanating from that country ever since the peace settlement was arranged in 1954.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, South Viet Nam constitutes a dangerous situation in the world today. But what happens if we do negotiate with the Chinese? Peace today cannot be attained quite so simply as that. I say that because, as far as the goal of the Chinese communists is concerned, negotiation with them would mean just about as much as their word meant when they said they would respect the international agreement which was made in 1954. Suppose we say, along with some others in the world today, that the United States should get out of South Viet Nam. What would happen? Do the communists take over the country? What about Laos and Cambodia? What about Thailand and Burma? And what about Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, New Zealand, Australia, India? I might go a little further and ask, what about ourselves?
I urge the Canadian government to give leadership because I believe leadership is something that Canada can give. I do not think leadership necessarily means appeasement. I do not think leadership necessarily means barking at the United States, trying to lay all the blame on their doorstep, either. I believe it is time to stand up for morality and the basic things which bring about peace, namely honour, trust and confidence in each other, not only between individuals but be-

tween nations as well. One of the tragedies in this whole Viet Nam situation is simply that North Viet Nam refuses to give that respect and honour to a sister nation which has been officially recognized, South Viet Nam.
And so, Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of our party, I am grateful that our member of the control commission did see fit to make a minority report. We should like to have more information about the entire situation. We urge the government to give this information to the house as long as it does not interfere with any positive program for peace and for an honourable settlement. Again I say that Canada, if she is going to act consistently with the reputation she has established throughout the years and for which she is respected, can only maintain that reputation if she stands up for these things which are right and moral, instead of kidding ourselves into thinking that there is a short cut to any lasting peace settlement.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-TABLING OF REPORTS OF CONTROL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that like other hon. members, our group would certainly like nothing better than to see peace achieved in Viet Nam.
However, the people, the army, in other words the government of North Viet Nam certainly have responsibilities in this war, since it has been proven that supplies and arms were sent through North Viet Nam to South Viet Nam, which is certainly interested in keeping up this war until victory is achieved.
On the other hand, the United States and South Viet Nam are quite prepared to bargain, as long as it is from a position of strength, having the upper hand at the start of the negotiations. Those two groups therefore want to intimidate one another through military force.
On the other hand, we have to bear in mind that the people of South Viet Nam are apparently not entirely satisfied with their present form of government, for they are having one revolution after another, one change of government after another. As a matter of fact, we can see that there is no stability within South Viet Nam, since South Vietnamese are not accepting the governments which seem to be imposed on them and which they are apparently determined to change regularly.
Under the circumstances, what stand should Canada take? Canada, as it has shown
Viet Nam Control Commission in the past, is seeking peace and, therefore, trying to find solutions to bring about peace, not by military force but through negotiation or by sending peace forces in the various countries where similar situations may exist.
As pointed out a moment ago, to be successful such a peace force would have to be large enough, perhaps too large.
A solution remains. There are countries, even powerful countries, in the western world as well as in the communist world advocating negotiations. France, on the one hand, and Russia, on the other, are favouring negotiations between those two groups who would be quite willing to fight it out until total victory.
Under the circumstances I think the best stand Canada could take would be to support those countries suggesting that negotiations should be held.
It must be borne in mind, for instance, that the communist bloc is divided. In fact, Russia and red China do not appear to be able to get together on what stand to take.
Both will of course blame North Viet Nam bombardment by the United States, but it will only be to save the face of Russia. However, it must be recognized that in certain fields Russia and communist China do not agree on what stand to take.
Therefore, why not take advantage of the stand taken by France and Russia who are ready to act as go-between in the negotiations? Then, it is clear that the United States would probably have to accept negotiations inasmuch as they have not got the upper hand, military speaking. But then, there would be a chance to avoid an all-out war.
Everyone should not always be expected to negotiate from military strength or from strength, period. If the United States stick to that policy of strength, communist China will come to the assistance of North Viet Nam and if there are no negotiations Russia will come to the assistance of China. That will give rise to an all-out war.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, our group believes that Canada must support those countries asking for negotiations on the war now going on in Viet Nam. We think that at the present time Canada is not in a position to set up with other countries a peace corps that would be sufficient to bring back peace in Viet Nam. That is why we think that the best position to take today is to follow those countries who want to negotiate a cease-fire where both sides would remain on their own position. I am convinced that the United Nations can obtain such a cease-fire. Besides, Russia in the communist camp, and France in the west-

Questions
ern camp, are both advocating such negotiations with the great powers involved. Therefore, the United Nations can obtain such a cease-fire and preside over negotiations between both sides. I think it is the only chance to reach a peaceful solution in southeast Asia.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I asked a number of questions during my remarks following the report by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I should now like to ask the Prime Minister what response he received to his proposal to the secretary general, and did the secretary general decide, following those discussions, to canvass some of the powers to ascertain whether they would join in the proposal? I should also like to ask how many men the Prime Minister envisages would be necessary to be mobilized in order to discharge the responsibilities that would be theirs in Viet Nam.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REPORTED PROPOSAL BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first place I think I should point out that there were no concrete proposals made by me in New York, no more than there were any made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs today. I put forward some ideas in New York, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs put forward some ideas today. I might add that we put forward some ideas at an earlier date, which we thought might be helpful in bringing peace to southeast Asia, and especially to Viet Nam, on the basis of agreed negotiated settlement.


So far as these ideas are concerned, the discussions I had with the secretary general were of a general nature. The United Nations itself was not mentioned in connection with those ideas because, if there is to be any negotiation, it might be that the negotiation machinery will not be that of the United Nations, any more than it was in 1954. However, the United Nations could be brought into the situation if the countries directly concerned so desired. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the question in respect of any particular national commitment does not arise at this stage.
The ideas I put forward have been sent to various countries, but we have not received any comment on them as yet, except from Washington, which has expressed interest in these ideas. I think Washington has described them as perhaps useful and constructive under the circumstances.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it would be premature to talk about any particular national commitment in respect of things which would depend entirely on a form of negotiation being worked out by the countries directly and immediately concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister must have had in mind some number of men which would be required to be mobilized to achieve the objective he has in mind. That is the reason I asked the question, because otherwise, I suggest, the thing would simply be fantasy.
I would therefore ask the Prime Minister if there has been any suggestion at all, based on any authentic information received from embassies in communist China or missions in North Viet Nam, to the effect that communist China or the government at Hanoi would be prepared to meet in any kind of conference for the purpose of giving consideration to the inception of negotiations.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no information at the moment which would give me any reason to conclude what would be the attitude of communist China or the government at Hanoi toward a definite proposal for negotiations.
In so far as the first part of the question is concerned, it would be quite impossible to indicate the number of men which would be required in any particular peace keeping operation until one had been able to ascertain what would be the political agreements under which they would be supervised and controlled. If all the countries in the area were wholeheartedly in favour of a settle-

ment, including the two governments of Viet Nam, perhaps the number of men required for such a force would be relatively small. However, this would depend entirely on the kind of settlement reached.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, with the indulgence of the house may I reply to a question asked last week by the hon. member for Timmins with respect to services made available to members discharged from the armed services, covering re-employment in the civilian labour force.
The discharge of members from the forces has needed and received an intensification of programs which had already been established as a result of earlier discussions between the national employment service and the forces. Facilities for counselling and aiding members of the navy, army and air force to prepare for the transition have been intensified, and the national employment service provides service counsellors with labour market and occupational information. The services provide detailed information to the national employment service about individual servicemen prior to their discharge. It is sometimes possible to provide civilian employment before the ex-serviceman receives his discharge.
In co-operation with the three services the national employment service has prepared comprehensive handbooks relating service trades and officer employment to civilian occupation, and is now preparing a series of job briefs to be supplied to service personnel on release, to help them interpret to civilian employers the value of the training and experience they have received in the service.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: When the committee rose on Friday last clause 6 of the bill was being considered with an amendment thereto by the hon. member for Beauce.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following the debate of last Friday and certain statements made today in this chamber, I must be more explicit on some points concerning the amendment and its bearing.
In opposition to what the newspapers reported during the week end, the amendment is devised only to allow a province, which exercises its constitutional right, to legislate in the field of social security, and more particularly concerning contributory benefits, and not to allow all the provinces to legislate or to negotiate agreements with other provinces.
Therefore, while we are studying this amendment, I wish to state strongly that this bill was presented to us mostly as a measure concerning nine provinces of Canada. This is obvious if we refer to what has been said on several occasions since the house unanimously adopted the principle of this bill on first and second reading. Besides I wish to make a correction in that respect. When the resolution was presented, nine members of the Ralliement Creditistes in the house voted against it-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Order. I ask the hon. member to limit his remarks to the amendment he moved and which is now under consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
That is precisely what I am doing. We claim under this amendment that Quebec, the only province which does not accept Bill No. C-136 in general, is entitled to conclude agreements with foreign states. We were often told that Quebec would have its own plan. We had nine who voted against the principle of compulsion and contributions included in this Bill No. C-138. I wish to make this correction, because it was often said that this was adopted unanimously when second reading was given in this house.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare claimed that we should proceed rapidly because this bill is very long, very complicated and concerns mostly the nine English speaking provinces of Canada.
Then, Mr. Chairman, if you refer to previous discussions, you will see that we abstained from voting in order not to delay the study of Bill No. C-136 in committee, so it could be passed in the interests of the
Canada Pension Plan
provinces who desired it. But we did not admit that this bill deprived citizens from the province of Quebec which will soon pass legislation in the field of social security.
Now that this bill has been sent back, we find that many of its sections are in complete contradiction with the Canadian constitution.
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of my amendment, which you stated to be in order, is to protect the rights of Quebec. It was admitted that legislation concerning old age security, on a contributory basis, came under the provinces, but that parliament, and therefore the House of Commons, had passed an amendment to the constitution. It v/as not said, however, that this would be a contributory plan, but that its purpose was to establish in Canada a pension plan which, according to the white paper, would permit the largest possible number of Canadians to retire with security and dignity. There was no question of contribution and obligation, there was no question either of an accumulated fund totalling $7 to $8 billion for the nine provinces directly involved in the bill in question.
But who has the right to legislate in this way?
I submit that my amendment is very important. Today, the Liberal members from the province of Quebec keep quiet, and even pretend that the member for Beauce acts in collusion with the Conservative party in order to delay the passing of this bill. Those members will certainly be blamed by their constituents for having allowed once more, by the passage of this bill, the citizens of the province of Quebec and their government to be deprived of the right to enjoy fully, totally and without limitation what has been recognized by them, for many years, by the constitution.
I might add, to prove my point, that this legislation is a purely provincial one. My amendment is important. In 1941, if I remember correctly, the constitution had to be amended to enable the federal government to legislate in the field of labour security by the establishment of a contributory unemployment insurance scheme. This could be an important case in point, because the authorization we gave could also apply to Bill No. C-136.
I maintain that the federal government is incapacitated in this matter, but not from a legal point of view. I know that, under the 1941 amendment, it is authorized to negotiate agreements with the states of Maine, Vermont or any foreign states to enable

Canada Pension Plan
people from Quebec to benefit from unemployment insurance. But I maintain that we have here a case of political incapacity.
It is probably because of political interest that every year for 24 or 25 years, about 6,000, 7,000 or 8,000 people lose their right to unemployment insurance benefits because the federal government alone was authorized to legislate and to enter into agreements with foreign countries concerning the social security of workers.
That is why I maintain that the province of Quebec should be given the right to negotiate with foreign provinces concerning its pension plan. Bill No. C-136 must stipulate specifically that the province of Quebec has the right to negotiate freely. This would not create a precedent; there has already been a precedent in that matter not later than last week. In fact, France considered that, from a legal standpoint, the province of Quebec had in the field of education the exclusive right to negotiate or to enter into an agreement concerning the exchange of professors between the province of Quebec, through its minister of education, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, and France, through its representative, Mr. Fouchet.
Hence we would not create a precedent by allowing, through an amendment to Bill No. C-136, the province of Quebec to negotiate by itself.
I shall quote professors of constitutional law, concerning a strictly Canadian and not foreign political matter, in support of the validity and the importance of my amendment. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to
argue a point which was advanced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni on Friday concerning the relationship of Indian people to this bill. I refer particularly to those Indians who earn their income from employment on the reserve. I believe the answer the minister gave on Friday was fairly clear, namely that if an Indian earned income from the use of reserve lands or from working on the reserve, then he would have no opportunity to contribute to the Canada pension fund from his earnings derived in that way. However, if he had income from employment which was otherwise pensionable employment, which was outside the boundaries of the reserve, then he would be eligible the same as everyone else is.
Some years ago, the official policy of the government, which was headed by the Liberal party at the time, was to try to entice native Indian people to cease being Indians within the meaning of the Indian Act, or otherwise to become enfranchised. They sought to entice them away from their position as native Indians under the Indian Act by way of discriminatory legislation. One of the methods used was the enticement of the right to vote. It was the Liberal party that said to the Indian people, you can have the right to vote in federal elections if you will give up your right to taxation exemptions on money earned on the reserve or from the use of reserve lands. Another enticement was liquor rights. The Liberal government some years ago said to the native people, you can have the right to consume liquor the same as everybody else, provided you give up your hereditary position as native Indians under the Indian Act, become enfranchised and leave the reserve. There were other en-

ticements, and there still are some enticements to the native Indian people to cease their existence as Indians under the Indian Act.
I submit this scheme is part and parcel of the same sort of discriminatory legislation. Under the bill that is before us now, if a native Indian earns his income from the use of reserve lands or from employment on the reserve-this is becoming increasingly more prevalent with the desire for economic development of the reserves-he will not be able to participate in the Canada pension scheme as other Canadians will be able to do. If he desires to participate fully in the Canada pension scheme, all he has to do is cease existence as an Indian under the Indian Act and then he will become entitled to participate, just as the non-Indian people are entitled to do.
I submit this is the same sort of disgraceful discriminatory legislation that the Liberal party put into effect not too many years ago and which they tried to use in order to entice the native people away from their natural way of living and from their situation as defined in the Indian Act. This legislation has the same objective, the same goal. At the same time on the west coast, for example, there are many Indian people who work part of the year on the reserve. Some of them have stores and others set up small businesses such as poolrooms on reserve lands. Some of them engage in logging activities, logging the timber on their own reserves. In fact one of the developments within the last four or five years, particularly within the Indian affairs branch, has been the economic development section. This section is evidence of the conscious desire of the Indian affairs branch to promote industrial development on the reserves. Many of these people spend part of the year working as loggers or in some other field on the reserve, and the other part of the year they live and work outside of the reserve, notably in the fishing industry. This means that only part of a person's income will be subject to contributions to the pension plan, inasmuch as it is an earnings related scheme. Since the Indian may work part of the time on the reserve and part of the time off the reserve, only a portion of his earnings will be applicable to the pension scheme. The portion applicable to the scheme over a period of years will be relatively small because all of his income will not be subject to contributions under the plan.
I submit the minister should look seriously at this situation, even though it may invoke
Canada Pension Plan
an amendment to two clauses. Some sort of approach should be made to make sure that legislation such as this is universally applicable. The proposal was that it would be universally applicable and that it would be completely portable, that no one would be excluded from it except by reason of his income being below a certain amount. There were certain other exclusions as well. Here, however, you have an exclusion based on racial inheritance. Surely in any legislation which the parliament of Canada enacts and which provides a benefit to the people of Canada, there should be no exclusion because of an individual's race. However this is precisely what this particular bill is doing.
What should occur, I submit, is this: Because of the unique position the native Indian people have in our society, because of the fact they have a position of pre-eminence because they were here long before anybody else, and because in all lands the so-called aboriginals have been given preferential treatment by the people who came from other lands, there should be some preferential treatment here.
But apart from this there should be complete equality of application of the law, and that is not what this bill seeks to do. By taking into account our usual desire to make sure that we treat fairly native Indians, the law should be amended to read simply that if the individual or band so desires, he or they will have the opportunity or right to opt into this plan and say, "Yes, we want to participate with other Canadians in the Canada pension fund. We want to contribute the same as other Canadians do. We want to expect the full benefits, as other Canadians do, when our time comes to receive those benefits under the plan."
If they have not already done so I urge the minister and the government to look at this from a policy point of view and make some pronouncement so that many of our Indian people who did not realize this existed -in fact no one realized it existed until the hon. member for Comox-Alberni tried to elicit some information about it-will be told that the government will change its mind and that they can expect it to deal fairly with them. The native Indian people have a hereditary right to participate or not, as they so wish.
I know there were some groans raised when I rose to speak, but this is a serious matter and I think the minister should go a little beyond what he said on Friday last when all he had to declare was that a factual situation existed. He did not go into the

Canada Pension Plan
question of the government's changing its mind with respect to that factual situation. We are entitled to some declaration of the government's intentions with respect to this matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The problem raised by my hon. friend is really one to be dealt with under clause 11 or 13. The question was originally raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in the hon. member's absence and, as will be found at page 12048 of Hansard, I gave the answers to which my hon. friend has referred.
The Canada pension plan is based upon income of individuals, and income, as used in the Canada pension plan bill, is based upon income as determined under the Income Tax Act. Under that act income earned by Indians on a reserve is excluded. If we want to proceed with this legislation on the premise that income will be determined on a different basis than that set forth in the Income Tax Act, then that is an entirely different matter from what is being dealt with in this legislation. If the government in its wisdom decided to change the basis of determining income under this bill as compared with the Income Tax Act, then my hon. friends' question would be a reasonable one.
What I indicated in my answer is that income under this bill is income as determined under the Income Tax Act. This automatically excludes the income which Indians earn on a reserve, on which they enjoy the benefit of not having to pay the normal taxes which apply in the case of individuals working outside a reserve. There is no provision for including income earned by Indians on reserves for the purposes of the Canada pension plan and excluding it for the purposes of the Income Tax Act.
This is the situation as it stands at present. I do not think it would be fair for me to make a statement with regard to future government policy on this matter, because the matter of income earned by Indians on a reserve is one provided for under the provisions of the Indian Act. If the government in the future decided to change the definition of income under this bill that would be a matter for government policy and, as I explained to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, though such income might still be excluded from the Income Tax Act, this could be done by the federal government acting on its own.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I think we can draw a reasonably distinct difference between the two situations. The exemption provisions in the Indian Act are recognition of the special status which

Indian people have in Canada. The legislation we are considering is of a welfare nature, so-called, broad in application, excluding no one on the basis of national extraction, and is in precisely the same category as our payments under the Old Age Security Act, except one is a flat rate and one is earnings related.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: My hon. friend may permit me to point out that income earned on a reserve is not included in taxable income for the purposes of O.A.S. Indians on reserves benefit from old age security, youth allowances and family allowances, all of which are paid out of general taxation revenue. This is quite a different situation from a pension plan based on contributions based on contributory earnings. As I mentioned, contributory earnings under this plan are determined as under the Income Tax Act. Any variance from this would require an amendment to this bill and a change in the principles involved in basing earnings on income under the Income Tax Act. If some government in the future decided to take such a step it would be a major one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
That is almost what I was getting to, that native Indian people do not pay income tax while earning on a reserve and, as a consequence, they do not pay a percentage of income tax into the old age security fund, but they are treated equally in the matter of benefits under it. The same is true with welfare payments, old age assistance, blind persons allowances and all the other payments, and where native Indian people do not pay tax on such income it is a recognition of their hereditary position.
I understand Indians make unemployment insurance contributions from income earned on reserves, in order to participate fully in the unemployment insurance benefits, so in that situation a different approach is taken in determining what is and what is not income. They are not subject to taxation under the Income Tax Act but they do make unemployment insurance fund contributions.
I am sure one could argue each side of this case with equal facility. I am not discounting the minister's arguments except to say that they are incorrectly based. What is required from the government is simply a look at the question as to whether we should treat for the purposes of a plan such as this, which, with some exceptions in other respects, is universally applicable to all of Canada, should we look on something which is a benefit from society to itself, with the government being a sort of intermediary, in an entirely different light when considering the question of the

hereditary rights of Indians to freedom from taxation on reserves income?
I submit that the two points must be looked at differently, and once you do that you can very easily come to the conclusion that you treat income under the pension bill in a different way than under the Income Tax Act.
Either the government looked carefully at this particular question beforehand and, having done so, decided to enact legislation which is discriminatory on a racial basis, or it did not look at the question at all and is just now being confronted with the problems involved in it. The minister's answer was clear, that he and his government have no intention of altering this bill, and consequently native Indian people will receive less benefits from the Canada pension plan than other Canadians. To me that is discrimination based on race.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I would simply like to point out that this bill is no more discriminatory toward Indians than it is toward married women, who may very well contribute to the earnings of their husbands.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: But married women are of a variety of races.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I will agree with that; but this is no more discriminatory of Indians who have exempt income under the Income Tax Act than it is of married women who may very well contribute toward the earnings of their husbands. There is just as good an argument to be made that one should say part of a husband's earnings are attributable to his wife, and that therefore she should be allowed to contribute to the Canada pension plan and benefit from it, as there is with respect to the Indians as mentioned by my hon. friend.
However, I would point out to my hon. friend that when moving into legislation such as this, as an initial basis it would be very dangerous to move from the determination of income as it is under the Income Tax Act. The amounts people are going to have to pay into this plan depends upon their earnings, that is, their wages, if they are employed by someone else, and their self-employed earnings if they are not working for someone else. Under the Income Tax Act it has taken a good deal of time and jurisprudence in Canada to determine what is income as defined under that act.
If my hon. friend is suggesting that one should move into this legislation and say that income, for the purposes of this legislation, should be income as determined by the
Canada Pension Plan
Income Tax Act except for the exemption with respect to Indians, I would submit to my hon. friend that this is only the beginning of exceptions, and that one could argue for all sorts of things to be changed in the determination of income under this act as compared with the Income Tax Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might just for a moment or two return to the question which was being discussed between the minister and the hon. member for Skeena. I must say that for some reason or another the Minister of National Revenue appears to have the matter of married women on his mind. This is the second time I have heard him advance this argument about a comparison between the status of certain people and that of married women. I say at once that I find his argument in connection with the Indian people very unconvincing. Quite frankly, I think it is a specious argument.
The minister will recall that when I asked questions on this subject on Friday, I did so purely from the point of view of getting a picture, in my mind at least, of what are the facts of the situation. I did not pursue the matter any further at that time because I recognize that this is a complex question, and up to a point I am willing to agree with the

Canada Pension Plan
minister that the question of departing from the principle of determining income as it is determined under the Income Tax Act could have its complications. But I have had an opportunity since Friday of reflecting upon the situation which the minister, quite properly, laid out in a factual way in answer to my questions. I think the point the hon. member for Skeena was trying to drive home, and which I would like to second, is that the Indian people have a peculiar status in our Canadian society. By "peculiar" I mean one that is separate and distinct from that of any other group in our society.
I would be prepared to argue that by making provision for income derived by Indians from their reserves as being pensionable income the minister would not be opening a Pandora's box that he was suggesting might be opened, because there is nobody else in Canada that has this status. I think we all recognize, without embarking upon a long speech, the reasons for that.
I am inclined to the view that the government-particularly from what the minister has said-has simply not really considered this question as a government. I for one would not expect the Minister of National Revenue to stand up here right now and make a commitment on behalf of the government, but there is one commitment I would like to have the minister make to the house. The Minister of National Revenue, because of his portfolio, has a preoccupation with income tax matters and things of that sort, but nevertheless I would like to have a commitment from him that he will take this matter up with his colleagues; that he will take it up with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the superintendent general of Indian affairs, who is charged with launching a community economic development program for the Indian people which we hope will result in the economic development on Indian reserves being a more important factor in the future.
If he will give us that commitment, or the assurance that this matter will be brought before the government for consideration, then perhaps we might be satisfied. We want him to recognize that this is a very special situation and that it is one deserving of special attention because of the obvious restriction on the ability of the Indian people to participate fully in a contributory pension plan. Here we have an opportunity of encouraging the Indian people to participate along with other Canadian citizens in a universal contributory pension plan, and by the very nature

of the restrictions that are imposed by the legislation as it is drafted, we are in effect encouraging them to shrink back, as far as this aspect of Canadian life is concerned, into their shells and not to go along with the rest of us in participating.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would first of all like to mention to my hon. friend that one would be opening some sort of Pandora's box, as he mentioned, if one took this particular step of saying that something that was not treated as income under the Income Tax Act should be treated as income under this act. In particular I would refer him to section 10 of the Income Tax Act, which has a great number of exceptions which one could argue should be taken as income for the purposes of the Canada pension plan. However, I would be glad to undertake to my hon. friend to bring the particular problem involved to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. This could be taken up with the people involved at the earliest opportunity when he is meeting with them to discuss the problems and of Indians generally being able to move into this plan, not on an individual basis but on an over-all basis, which I think would have to be done, in all fairness, in dealing with this particular situation. I would be very pleased to raise this question with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
