Mr. Chairman, just before we pass this clause I would like to say this.
I think throughout all this discussion the minister has an incorrect base from which to start considering this particular question. He persistently refers to what is classified as income under the Income Tax Act. I think if he would only confer with the hon. lady sitting next to him-whose name in the Indian tongue escapes me at the moment, but who is fairly close to the native people and spent a memorable few moments out in my own part of the country a few years ago- she will be able to explain to the minister that these are people; they are not earnings under the Income Tax Act. This is the principle upon which this question has to be looked at, namely that we are concerning ourselves with people here, a particular group of people, a group of people that by far should get prior consideration when we are dealing in this parliament with their welfare and rights.
We are dealing with people who really have received pretty scant attention in years past. This is the basis upon which we must look at this question; not from the

point of view of what is some legalistic definition of earnings under the Income Tax Act, or what is somebody else's conception of how you should draft statute law in the particular bill that is now before us. We are dealing primarily with a group of people who, as I said, deserve prior consideration and a greater amount of concern than anybody else. If the minister approaches it from this point of view, and if the government approaches it from this point of view, they will make their task very easy and will not discover this so-called Pandora's box, or whatever it is. The minister has an aptness for phraseology that is not too good sometimes, and I do not think many of the Indian people, except the female ones, that I know of will like to be termed as married women, or as the same thing as married women. They will have some reaction against that. But the minister is drawing poor comparisons when he tries to compare an individual, who has a distinct position in this nation, an individual who has a particular racial inheritance, with the broad, general category of married women.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend is not suggesting that there is anything inferior about the broad group of married women in the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The hon. lady not being one herself, she might have a different attitude than I about this. But the fact is that the minister has drawn this distinction and has tried to compare a group of people with a distinct racial inheritance with one section of the general public which he classifies as married women. I think he is trying to compare things which are not comparable. He should be talking about native Indian people pure and simple. If the minister and the government do this, they will come to the conclusion, and I submit the correct conclusion, that all people should be treated fairly. There should be no distinction on the basis of race in an application of law such as this, which is universal or supposedly universal in application all across the nation.
By way of illustration, say one Indian earns his entire income of $5,000 over, say, a period of 10 years, reaches the age of 65 and retires. If his income is derived entirely from work on the reserve he will have a pension of $104. But another who earns half the same income, namely $2,500, from fishing-in which case he will pay twice as much as most other people because the government have already decided a while ago that they wanted to dis-
Canada Pension Plan
criminate against fishermen

and the other half of his income from logging on the reserve, and who likewise contributes for 10 years and retires at age 65, will have a pension of $52, or half that of the first person. This is inequity before the law and inequity based on race.
I would ask the minister to look at the question, not in face of the terminology of the Income Tax Act or any other act-it is not a definition of what is or is not earnings under some other law that is important here -but on the basis of a particular group of people. If he and the government sincerely start from there they will have no difficulty in producing some legislation which treats all people fairly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would care to tell us if this particular aspect of the plan about which we are talking was thoroughly explored, and if so, why is it that some Indian people who live on reservations and who earn most of their income on the reservation have for some reason been left out? Was it decided that their earnings would be treated, for the purposes of this plan, in the same way as they are treated under the Income Tax Act? If so, I am wondering whether the reason the Indian people may not qualify was on account of the fact that it was determined that the average earnings of these people would not put them in the wage brackets which would make them taxable under this plan. I should like the minister to tell us whether this question was fully looked into when the plan was being drawn up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in drawing up this plan it was decided that the only logical basis on which to institute a plan such as this without all sorts of definitions of "earnings", and other things which are quite unrelated to the determination of income under the Income Tax Act, was to adopt the general policy that income under this act would be the same as income as determined under the Income Tax Act. I can assure my hon. friend and also the hon. member who spoke before him that in the drafting of this legislation there was no intention to discriminate against any sort of person in Canada because of race, colour, creed or marital status. It was simply because, on the basis of legislation like this which is going to cover such a vast number of people in Canada and which has to be administered by my department, the sound and logical basis on which to base the legislation was to use the same definition of "income" as that used

Canada Pension Plan
under the Income Tax Act. This obviates taking one's income as determined under the Income Tax Act and then making all sorts of adjustments in order to arrive at the amount on which a contribution is made to the Canada pension plan. I believe the plan would become almost administratively impossible, or you might have to set up a separate administrative procedure, if you were to vary greatly from the determination of income for the purposes of this act as compared with the determination of income for the purposes of the Income Tax Act.

speechtext:
This may have been justified at the time the plan was drafted, but I am thinking of the future, and the not too distant future at that. At the present time, in the constituency I represent there are a goodly number of needy Indians, not many of whom would qualify for the plan, but who might be able to contribute to the plan from earnings on the reservations. However, under new plans of community development and in view of the desirability of bringing some kind of industry into the reservation areas it is to be hoped that this drastic situation will not continue for very long and that we will be able to supplement the earnings of these Indian people. Therefore I support the hon. member for Skeena in his plea that the minister take a very close look at this question. Because here is a plan which the government says is an adequate pension plan. In a few years, if these Indian people gradually reach the stage which enables them to earn a substantial income on their reservations but nothing is done to include them in the plan or to make some change whereby earnings for the purposes of this plan are not considered to be the same as earnings under the Income Tax Act, then they will be placed in a very tragic and difficult situation.
I am not maintaining that the plan is discriminatory. In fact, that was the minister's word. He said that he did not think that the plan was any more discriminatory against the Indians than it was against married women. Perhaps he can tell us whether this plan is discriminatory against married women.

Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to clause 7 which I hope will be considered consequential and will pass as readily as the one which has just been moved from the other side of the house. The minister may recall that earlier in our discussion of clause 2 reference was made to the situation of the fishermen in relation to the coverage provided by the Canada pension plan. During the discussion the minister made particular reference to the provisions of clause 7. I will not go through all his remarks which were made at that time, but generally speaking he drew attention to the
fact that under clause 7 the governor in council is entitled to make regulations to permit inclusions in pensionable employment, under certain terms and conditions. This had particular reference to clause 7 (1) (c), which reads:
-any employment if it appears to the governor in council that the nature of the work performed is similar to the work performed by persons employed in pensionable employment;
My amendment arises out of the fact- this matter was touched on in the earlier discussion-that in the Unemployment Insurance Act the rather parallel provisions therein gave the governor in council the power to bring fishermen within the coverage of that act. In spite of the arguments we advanced, this power was never exercised until finally a specific amendment was introduced to the Unemployment Insurance Act which had the result of bringing fishermen, who might not be in the position of enjoying the ordinary employee-employer relationship, under the coverage of unemployment insurance.
It is arising out of that experience that I should like to move what I hope the minister will consider a consequential amendment which will clarify and make perfectly clear the situation as far as fishermen are concerned. I do so because of the fact that the minister, and following his lead the house generally, refused to accept certain amendments proposed by the hon. member for Skeena which would have changed the definition of "employee" and "employer" in the definition clause. The minister argued at the time that the situation of fishermen in all parts of the country was not exactly parallel, and that there should be some flexibility in the manner in which the act would be applied to them in relation to whether or not they should be considered as employees.
Therefore, I now move:
That clause 7 of Bill No. C-136 be amended by adding thereto a new subclause (4) as follows:
"(4) (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this act the governor in council may make regulations for including employment in fishing for all purposes of this act.
(b) For purposes of this subclause a fisherman may be deemed to be an employee notwithstanding that he is not an employee of any other person, and any person with whom the fisherman enters into a contractual or other commercial relationship in respect of his occupation as a fisherman may be deemed to be an employer."
This, Mr. Chairman, is a permissive piece of legislation if it is inserted into the bill, but I would construe it to have something of the same force and effect as the amendment in-

Canada Pension Plan
troduced in 1956 to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which is closely similar in that it specifically authorized the governor in council to approve regulations made by the unemployment insurance commission to include employment in fishing in insurable employment. As far as I was able, I have drafted my amendment to the pension legislation in a form parallel with that which was drafted as an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act, as passed by the house in 1956, for a somewhat related purpose.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to pursue the argument on behalf of my amendment at any length because we did explore this question when we had clause 2 under consideration. However, I feel the amendment I have now proposed has been designed to meet the objections raised at the time we were considering clause 2 in respect of the early amendment we proposed, on the basis of its being too rigid. I believe this amendment allows for that flexibility which the minister has suggested is necessary, while at the same time makes clear, if this amendment passes, that the intention of parliament is that the governor in council shall give recognition to the rather special circumstances which pertain to the fishing industry in many areas, but particularly on the west coast where for practical purposes the relationship of fishermen, as independent operators, to those to whom they sell their fish, is one of employee and employer, because in a great many cases they are chartering or buying boats from these people to whom they sell their fish. On that basis, Mr. Chairman, I feel that this amendment should be regarded as a necessary consequential amendment to the clause as originally proposed.

Mr. Chairman, under section 8, the employee shall pay 1.8 per cent of his pensionable earnings for the year, and the employer shall also pay 1.8 per cent of the same amount.
On this matter, I would like to point out that this amount of 1.8 per cent or practically 2 per cent of the salary of the Canadian worker, will be deducted from his pay cheque and turned over to the federal government which will apply it to some other plan.
The worker, Mr. Chairman, already has deductions made from his salary respecting his federal income tax, his provincial income tax, his union fees, his unemployment insurance, and other deductions respecting various pension or insurance plans. And now, it is proposed that a further amount of 1.8 per cent be taken from him. At the rate things are going, before long, the Canadian worker will probably prefer to draw his pay check stub rather than the check itself. More and more is being taken out of the worker's pay

envelope. He works to earn a salary but at the end of a week, two weeks, a month or a year, deductions are made from his pay for this and for that. And here is a new plan which takes a little more from the Canadian worker, which means that his pay will be a little smaller.
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that the way things are going, the government is trying to take everything away from the Canadian citizens. Why not let the worker keep what he earns and see to it that he gets a pension when he is 65? It should be possible to do both, Mr. Chairman. The worker should keep what he earns. Nothing more should be taken from him, as we are planning to do under clause 8 of Bill No. C-136. But we should give him a pension just the same. The government has now decided to raise the pension to $100 a month. Let us give him that and, if necessary, let us add to it, so that everybody will have the same pension, because under a plan of this type, it is those who earn most who will be the most favoured.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have the minister in the house during the time this question
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion is put. That is not the usual procedure. I see the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) also present. He is the hon. member who has described the minister as being the only man in the House of Commons who is not afraid of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), so it is a special thrill for me to face such a brave titan. The reason I want to get into the question I brought up on Friday is that it is even more significant-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON EFFECTS OF AUTOMATION
speechtext: Maybe he will answer.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON EFFECTS OF AUTOMATION
speechtext:
You mean that one punch may be giving the reply? We will wait and see.
The minister was quoted in Saturday's newspaper and on Monday, right after I raised the question on Friday, and if his comment is at all correct it just underlines the reason I should ask the question and why this house should expect an answer on that part of policy. If I get the gist of the minister's statement to this Liberal meeting at Newmarket, the world is in wonderful shape and things are easy. The only reason the Lucien Rivard case and matters like that come up in the House of Commons is that the opposition has not anything else to say. The economy is so great, unemployment has been solved, Hal Banks has been put in his place and all is right with the world. This is the minister's line. It is not good enough.
I want to contrast this, Mr. Speaker, with the minister's comment in the Financial Post of August 22, 1964. It started off this way:
The biggest question mark now hanging over employment and manpower is automation and technological change. These are things we cannot halt, even if we wanted to. Canada, like other countries, must take advantage of new techniques but in doing so we are determined to do everything in our power to see that, while we reap the benefits of these advances, we do not do so at the expense of the workers involved.
Then he goes on to talk about the wonderful manpower consultative service that is being set up. Well, Professor Deutsch of the Economic Council of Canada has published an annual report. He has kicked the daylights out of the manpower consultative service. I hope hon. members have read the portion of the report in which he indicates that this is an organization that is going to be operating in limbo. I think those are pretty close to his words. He indicated that while perhaps this manpower organization is an idealistic idea, it is not practical. The report is much more critical than that.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
However, I should like to turn to a recent quotation from the worthy professor. This statement appeared in the Toronto Star for January 27 and it is entitled, "Deutsch says: Don't have to put workers on shelf". I quote:
Until the point of perfection has been reached where everyone's needs and wants have been satisfied, there is no need to put people out of jobs and pay them to stay on the shelf, Dr. J. J. Deutsch of Ottawa, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, said here.
Dr. Deutsch, here to attend the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, said in an interview, "I can see no basic reason why we cannot keep expanding our production to meet unfilled needs and keep creating jobs to meet the increasing demands for production."
"Automation can increase production and make more goods available with less labour and enable us to hold our place in a competitive world market," he said.
More and more, the interpretation of Dr. Deutsch's study is being realized, and the other day the Globe and Mail of March 5 contained a story by Ronald Anderson which carries this title: "Hard-Core Theory of Jobless Levels Disputed in Study". I should like to quote part of the article:
The theory of structural unemployment-the idea that automation and other technological changes have created a hard core of unemployed-was dealt a stiff blow in a staff study released this week by the Economic Council of Canada.
The study contends there are no signs of an increase in so-called hard-core unemployment in the period since the second world war, except the increase associated with a rise in over-all unemployment.
Now, if that is true, as Mr. Anderson points out, this is more significant and it raises very many questions about this whole problem of technological change and automation, how serious the problem is, and what kind of policies we should have to meet it. My question is a fairly straightforward one to the minister: What are the government's policies in lieu of an analysis presented by the Economic Council of Canada, particularly its criticism of the manpower consultative service, particularly its criticism both in that report and in these other studies, particularly the Windsor study, which indicates that our unemployed are not really getting into the retraining and training program? It seems to me we deserve an answer from the minister longer than the three minutes he can give us.
I would make a personal observation here to underline this, Mr. Speaker. I went into the library where they are good enough to keep files on all hon. members, and I would advise the minister to go in and have a look at the very substantial file built up in connec-

tion with himself. There are lots of stories on the minister talking about the likelihood of elections, about all kinds of fancy deals, about how Cape Breton should be happy, and about what a wonderful people the maritimers are. But there is a tremendous lack of stories and comments about the minister and the policy objectives of his own department.
I would like to suggest to him that if this is a fair kind of clipping it indicates he is not living up to his responsibilities as Minister of Labour, that he is not giving us a real lead in terms of policies and the whole question of technological change and automation.

I must say I shared the hon. member's view with respect to that section of the report which dealt with manpower policy in Canada, and which could have benefited hugely from a greater factual knowledge of what is actually being done in the manpower field, and which is not reflected in the report.
